metadata.note: The Elizabethtown, Lexington and Big Sandy (organized 1869) built Lexington - Winchester - Mt. Sterling in 1871-72 and leased it to the Louisville, Cincinnati and Lexington; Collis Huntington's Newport News & Mississippi Valley built on from Mt. Sterling to Denton/Seaton 1879-81, where it met the Ashland Coal & Iron's Ashland - Seaton line (ex-Lexington & Big Sandy Eastern Division), and the through Lexington - Ashland route opened in December 1881. The C&O operated it from early 1882 (Howard, 178 U.S. 153), took it by formal consolidation in Feb 1892, and ran it as the Lexington Subdivision until the last passenger trains (the Louisville section of the George Washington, trains 21/22) on 30 Apr / 1 May 1971. Three features: LC&L 1875-1880 on Lexington - Mt. Sterling; EL&BS 1881 [ANCHOR] and C&O 1882-1971 on Lexington - Ashland, sharing identical geometry (Rule 4 split at the date a source names the C&O as operator).
metadata.ownership_split: Lexington - Mt. Sterling: LC&L lessee June 1872 - c.1881. Through route: EL&BS / NN&MV Dec 1881; C&O operator from early 1882 (Howard) - the split used; 1886 leases to the Connecticut NN&MV Co. and the Feb 1892 consolidation are corporate only and are not splits; the C&O's 1925 lease / 1933 deed of the Ashland Coal & Iron (Ashland - Seaton track) did not change who ran the Lexington trains.
metadata.omitted: Not drawn: C&O trains Lexington - Frankfort - Louisville over the L&N by trackage rights (that track is ln_louisville_frankfort_lexington.geojson); Ashland - Big Sandy River / Catlettsburg (no confirmable EL&BS passenger year; C&O main line already drawn); the 1850s Lexington & Big Sandy Ashland - Coalton (no passenger evidence under that name); Lexington - Elizabethtown (never built); the Ashland Coal & Iron's own trains (1880 / 1917 anchors), Morehead & North Fork (1921 anchor), Kentucky & South Atlantic (1884 anchor) and the Salt Lick - Yale logging road (1902 anchor) - other companies, outside this layer. Ashland - Huntington is not duplicated: the line ends at Ashland station.
metadata.freight_only_check: No freight-only years drawn. After 1 May 1971 the line carried freight only (Lexington - Winchester lifted early 1980s; Winchester - Coalton abandoned 1984-85; Ashland - Coalton still in freight service) - none of that is drawn.
metadata.horsecar_check: None: the line was steam-worked from opening.
conflicts: Passenger END: 1971 adopted on dated last runs (lexhistory.org node/586: 30 Apr 1971 5:30 PM eastbound, 1 May 1971 8:05 AM westbound; Frankfort Union Station marker; Wikipedia). Rejected: abandonedrails.com 'mid 1950s' (contradicted by the Apr 1967 timetable with times - probably a confusion with the May 1957 Lexington Union Station closure); kygenweb Montgomery/Bath '1970' (contradicted by the dated runs); Carter County Railroads history '1972' (one year late; would overclaim).

LC&L START: 1875 drawn (Fowler 'y' = 1875 Official Guide). 1872 probable (rail to Mt. Sterling by June 1872; 1872 combined passenger and freight depot; Poor's 'in operation') but not timetable-confirmed.

MILEAGE: 'about 109 / over 109 miles' (Wikipedia C&O Lexington Subdivision; lexhistory.org) vs 123.7 (Fowler) and 124 timetable miles (C&O 1967 mileposts). The OSM trace gives ~123 mi, so 109 is wrong or measures something else. Carter County source's Denton MP 540.6 fits neither chain.
Lexington Union Station closure: May 1957 (Wikipedia) vs 'until 1959' (Fowler). Only affects the 1957 segment boundary, which is a station change, not a service change.

Ashland Coal & Iron control: Carter County history says the C&O 'gained control' of the AC&I in Dec 1881; Wikipedia dates C&O control 1924 / lease 1925. Either way the Lexington trains over Ashland - Seaton were EL&BS/C&O trains.
not_yet_sourced: 1872-1874 passenger service Lexington - Mt. Sterling (LC&L): probable, not timetable-confirmed; a Lexington or Mt. Sterling newspaper of 1872 (Chronicling America) would settle it. The LC&L feature's START is the first confirmed year, not a known start.
End of the LC&L lease of Lexington - Mt. Sterling: not found. Drawn to 1880 (the 1881 through-route opening year belongs to the EL&BS feature); LC&L operation probably ran into 1881.

1888-1892 operator: the C&O was reorganized in 1888 and the NN&MV Co. held the EL&BS lease until Feb 1892. Whether the reorganized C&O or an NN&MV operating organization ran the trains is not settled; drawn C&O (the 1889 FFV Lexington service suggests C&O-branded service) unless a source names another operator.
All headway_min and avg_speed_kmh values are estimates except the 1967 one-train-each-way frequency (Apr 1967 C&O timetable).
1894-1950: no year-by-year check; service rests on continuity between Fowler's 1890s Guide letters and the 1951 Guide table.
How through passengers reached Huntington 1881-1888, before the C&O's Catlettsburg - Kenova bridge, is not established.
Alignment changes 1881-1971 on the Lexington Subdivision were not researched; the line is drawn on its final alignment.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenStreetMap end to end, no straight-line legs: 123.4 mi drawn Lexington - Ashland. Documented mileage conflicts and the trace settles it: Fowler (branchline.uk Kentucky file, section 59) gives Ashland 0.0 - Lexington 123.7, and the Apr 1967 C&O timetable's mileposts give 124 (Ashland MP 453 - Lexington MP 577), both within 1% of the trace; Wikipedia's and lexhistory.org's 'about 109 / over 109 miles' does not fit and is recorded as a conflict in metadata. Intermediate check against the 1967 mileposts (from Ashland): Hitchins 26 vs 26.0 traced, Olive Hill 40 vs 41.1, Morehead 59 vs 59.2, Mt. Sterling 90 vs 91.2, Winchester 105 vs 106.4. Routed miles by OSM tagging: C&O 124.4 mi, OHM:(untagged) 0.2 mi - i.e. the whole route stayed on ways tagged old_railway_operator=C&O: live CSX track Ashland - Coalton (the surviving stub) and around Lexington/Winchester/Morehead, the rest lifted grade (Winchester - Coalton abandoned 1984-85; Lexington - Winchester lifted early 1980s, partly the Brighton East Rail Trail). Waypoints (Nominatim town points, every result's type checked; Lexington, the Lexington-east trail point and Ashland station hand-pinned) all lie within 0.7 km of the drawn line. Lexington end: the trace begins about 0.5 km short of the pinned Midland Avenue / Water Street point, on the C&O's approach along Midland Ave; the line is not drawn to any one of the C&O's successive Lexington stations (Water St 1872, Union Station to 1957, Water St freight depot 1957/59-1968, Delaware Ave 1968-71). Ashland end: Ashland station (the Amtrak/C&O station point); the last ~0.9 mi runs over the C&O Ohio River main line west of the station, which is also drawn by chesapeake_and_ohio.geojson (FFV / George Washington) - the shortest overlap that reaches the station. Kept distinct from the Lexington & Eastern / Kentucky Union: no mile of this trace is on L&N-tagged track (the L&E's own Lexington - Winchester line survives as CSX's CC Subdivision, south of this one). ALIGNMENT ERA: this is the line's final (1971) alignment as recorded in OSM. Any relocations between 1881 and 1971 were not researched, so the early years may be drawn on a later alignment in places; no specific relocation is known. The Ashland - Seaton (Denton) part is Ashland Coal & Iron track (Princess Tunnel), drawn as part of the through route because the Lexington trains ran over it.
properties.documented_mileage: 123.7 mi (Fowler s.59) / 124 timetable mi (C&O Apr 1967); conflicting 'about 109 mi' (Wikipedia, lexhistory.org)

segments.note: C&O operation of the EL&BS through route Lexington - Winchester - Mt. Sterling - Morehead - Olive Hill - Denton/Seaton, then Ashland Coal & Iron track via Princess Tunnel to Ashland. Start 1882: Chesapeake & Ohio Ry. v. Howard, 178 U.S. 153 (1900), names the C&O ('the Virginia company') as operating the Kentucky line 'for and on account of the Elizabethtown' from early 1882 - the Rule 4 split date. The 1886 paper leases of both roads to Huntington's Connecticut Newport News & Mississippi Valley Co. did not change who ran the trains (Howard: no real change of personnel or management). Fowler's section 59 'z' letters (1890 Official Guide) mark through stations over the whole route soon after. headway_min 720 (two trains each way daily) is an ESTIMATE, not from a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: Howard (178 U.S. 153) for C&O operation from early 1882; lexhistory.org for the Dec 1881 opening. Frequency not sourced.

segments.note: C&O Lexington - Ashland passenger service. 1889: the FFV was 'inaugurated' as an overnight Lexington - Tidewater/Washington service (lexhistory.org), and Fowler's section 59 marks every station Ashland - Lexington with 'z' (1890 Official Guide per the section header). Continued in the Feb 1952 Official Guide, Table 4 'Ashland-Lexington-Louisville' (schedule dated 31 Mar 1951), which lists Salt Lick, Olympia, Preston, Mt. Sterling, L.&E. Junction and Winchester with times - a rail table, not motor coach. No source dates frequency changes between 1889 and 1951; Fowler's letters stop at 1893 for this road, so 1894-1950 rests on continuity between the 1890s Guide and the 1951 Guide, not on a year-by-year check. Split at 1957 only because Lexington Union Station closed 9/10 May 1957 and the C&O moved to its Water Street freight depot (Wikipedia; Fowler says 1959). headway_min 720 is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: lexhistory.org (1889 FFV), Fowler section 59 (1890G letters) and the Feb 1952 Official Guide Table 4 name this service. 1894-1950 not checked year by year; frequency not sourced.

segments.note: Last C&O era. Apr 1967 C&O timetable: trains 21 (westbound, Ashland 5:05 AM) / 22, the Louisville section of the George Washington, split from the main train at Ashland, with times at Hitchins, Olive Hill, Morehead, Salt Lick, Preston, Mt. Sterling, Winchester and Lexington (streamlinerschedules.com) - one train each way daily, so headway_min 1440 is from that timetable for 1967 and an estimate for the other years. Lexington used the Water Street freight depot, then a new station at 1008 Delaware Ave from Dec 1968. Ends 1971: the last eastbound left Lexington 5:30 PM 30 Apr 1971 and the last westbound left for Frankfort and Louisville 8:05 AM 1 May 1971 (lexhistory.org node/586); Amtrak did not retain the route. Conflicting end dates (mid-1950s, 1970, 1972) are recorded in metadata and rejected. Freight continued: Lexington - Winchester lifted early 1980s, Winchester - Coalton abandoned 1984-85; Ashland - Coalton survives as freight track (not drawn).
sources: Segment-level: Apr 1967 C&O timetable (streamlinerschedules.com) for trains 21/22 and their frequency; lexhistory.org node/586 for the dated last runs 30 Apr / 1 May 1971.

segments.note: [ANCHOR] December 1881: the through route opened under the Elizabethtown, Lexington and Big Sandy's own name (built Mt. Sterling - Denton by Huntington's Newport News & Mississippi Valley 1879-81; last spike near Denton) - 'the first train ran ... Ashland to Lexington, over 109 miles' (lexhistory.org). From early 1882 the C&O operated the line (Howard), so the own-name era is a matter of weeks; it is drawn as the single year 1881 because the map's resolution is a year. Ashland - Seaton was Ashland Coal & Iron track used by these trains. The Lexington - Mt. Sterling part had carried LC&L-operated trains before 1881 (see the LC&L feature in this file). headway_min is an ESTIMATE; no 1881 timetable was seen.
sources: Segment-level: lexhistory.org for the Dec 1881 first through train; Howard (178 U.S. 153) for C&O operation from early 1882. Frequency not sourced.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenStreetMap, no straight-line legs: the Lexington - Mount Sterling part of the same opstrace route as the Lexington - Ashland features in this file, cut at the vertex nearest Nominatim's Mount Sterling point (0.25 km away). 32.2 mi drawn against 33.5 mi documented (Poor's Manual 1874/75 via Wikipedia; '33 miles', lexhistory.org). All on ways tagged old_railway_operator=C&O (lifted grade and the Brighton East Rail Trail east of Lexington, live track at the ends). ALIGNMENT ERA: drawn on the C&O's final alignment; the 1872 EL&BS line was the same corridor (Lexington - Winchester - Mt. Sterling) but any later relocations are not researched, and the Lexington end is the C&O's Midland Ave approach, not specifically the 1872 Water Street depot (about 0.5 km off the drawn line's start).

segments.note: Louisville, Cincinnati and Lexington (Railway from 1877, after receivership) trains over the Elizabethtown, Lexington and Big Sandy's Lexington - Winchester - Mt. Sterling line, which the LC&L operated under lease from June 1872 (revenue two-thirds to the operator, one-third to the owner - lexhistory.org; Poor's Manual 1874/75 via Wikipedia: 'in operation - Lexington to Mt. Sterling, 33.5 miles', leased to the LC&L). START 1875 is the first CONFIRMED passenger year: Fowler's 'y' (1875 Official Guide) letters on Mount Sterling, Thomson, Hedges, Winchester, Pine Grove and Comb's Ferry (Chilesburg). Service PROBABLY began in 1872 - rail reached Mt. Sterling by June 1872 and the 1872 Water Street depot was a 'combined passenger and freight depot' (lexhistory.org) - but no timetable shows it, so 1872-1874 is withheld. Do not widen without a timetable or newspaper. END: the date the LC&L lease ended is NOT established; the line became part of the EL&BS through route in Dec 1881 (and the LC&L passed to L&N control in 1881), so the lease ended by early 1882 at the latest. Drawn to 1880 so this feature does not overlap the 1881 EL&BS through-route feature on the same track; LC&L operation probably continued into 1881. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: Fowler section 59 (y = 1875 Official Guide) for the 1875 start; lexhistory.org for the 1872 lease. End year is an inference, not sourced.
